item.title: Feeling Trapped in Rush Hour Traffic? Discover How Mental Health Coaching Can Help You Stay Centered
item.description:
Few things remind us of how little control we have as well as rush hour traffic does. No matter how carefully you plan, congestion forces you to wait. It has a way of stealing more than just minutes from your day. It drains energy, patience, and sometimes even the good mood you started your day with. You may find help from mental health coaching.

Sitting behind the wheel, you may feel powerless as the line of cars stretches endlessly ahead. That lack of control can stir frustration, anxiety, and even anger. The thing is, the stress of traffic rarely stays in the car. It follows you into the office, into conversations with loved ones, and into the way you handle challenges later in the day. What begins with brake lights and honking horns ends with irritability and tension elsewhere.

Is it really worth ignoring, then? Mental health coaching is one helpful approach that helps to break that cycle and can keep you centered even when the road feels unpredictable.

The Bigger Problem Behind the Wheel

Traffic stress has a lot to do with the way our minds react to situations we cannot control. When we feel powerless, our bodies respond with tension, racing thoughts, and irritability. In time, this repeated stress response can make us more reactive in other areas of life.

The frustration you feel in traffic is likely the same you get when deadlines pile up or when family responsibilities feel too demanding. Many people fall into habits that make traffic stress even worse. Some examples include:

  • Constantly checking the clock and calculating how late they will be.
  • Replaying arguments or stressful conversations while sitting in the car.
  • Using the commute as a time to prepare mentally for conflict instead of being calm.
  • Letting small irritations, like someone cutting in, feel personal.

All of this only serves the purpose of keeping the stress cycle alive. This is why it would really help if you have a way to replace these responses with healthier ones that leave you calmer and more centered.

Mental Health Coaching for Better Ways to Stay Centered in Traffic

Instead of the usual advice like “take deep breaths,” mental health coaching encourages more creative approaches that fit into real life. Some helpful strategies that can make a surprising difference include:

Create a sensory reset Keep something simple in the car, like a calming scent or a textured object to hold. These small sensory cues remind your body to relax.

Turn the car into a learning space Use the time to listen to podcasts or audiobooks that genuinely interest you. This reframes the commute as personal growth rather than wasted time.

Rehearse calm responses Instead of replaying arguments, practice responding calmly in stressful situations. This builds resilience for challenges outside of traffic.

Set a transition ritual Decide on a short routine when you arrive, such as taking a short break before stepping out of the car. This helps you leave traffic stress behind rather than carry it into your next environment.

That said, trying new mental health habits is always easier when you have guidance. Mental health coaching provides accountability and perspective, helping you see where stress patterns show up and how to replace them with healthier ones.

A coach is there to help you connect the dots between traffic frustration and other areas of life, so you learn to respond differently in situations where control is limited. After a while, this builds a stronger sense of calm that extends far beyond the commute.

Traffic will always be part of modern life, but the way you respond to it doesn’t have to drain your energy. Mental health coaching is a great approach to help you reclaim peace in places where stress usually takes over, and those skills carry into every part of your day.

If you’re ready to talk more about building these centering habits, reach out to one of the mental health coaches listed on this site or call the numbers on the screen. Taking that step is a practical way to bring calm back into your daily drive and block out the mad rush noise.

item.title: Attachment Issues: Signs, Causes, Effects, and Ways to Overcome
item.description:
Who are you as you relate to the people around you? If you pause long enough to consider the patterns of behavior that mark your interactions with other people, you might surprise yourself. The way you build relationships with others may be rooted in and display attachment issues. This can negatively affect those relationships. Identifying any attachment issues you may have and working on them can help you nurture healthier connections.

Healthy Relationships and Attachment Issues

If healthy relationships can be described as being rooted in trust, mutual dependence, openness, and security, attachment issues result in relationships that don’t have an abundance of these qualities. When a person has attachment issues, it means they struggle to depend on, trust, or feel secure with other people in their lives.

To dig a little deeper, attachment issues can be described as the patterns of difficulty a person experiences in being able to form or maintain emotional bonds with other people. These patterns are often rooted in formative early life experiences. Whether through early life or later experiences, the patterns set in motion shape how one relates to family, partners, friends, and even colleagues.

The concept of attachment issues comes from John Bowlby’s research in the mid-20th century about the way the quality of the bond formed between a primary caregiver and the child in their care helps to influence that child’s social, emotional, and relational development throughout their life. An insecure bond between the child and their caregiver can result in an insecure attachment style, leading to attachment issues.

Attachment issues can make it hard to have healthy and meaningful relationships with other people.

Signs and Patterns of Attachment Issues

When you have attachment issues, they can differ and vary in terms of their intensity as well as the range of behaviors they produce. Any attachment issues you may have may be displayed through various behaviors in daily life, such as the following:

Dependency or clinginess This may look like feeling anxious if a loved one isn’t constantly available. If they don’t read or immediately respond to messages, or if you don’t know where they are or who they’re with, that can make you feel anxious. You might also feel anxious about their love and constantly ask them to reassure you or make gestures that indicate they care about you.

Fear of intimacy or closeness Pushing people away when they get too close, or avoiding deep relationships altogether, is another pattern of attachment issues. When a relationship starts getting deep or requires commitment and intimacy, it can start to feel uncomfortable, and it’s easier to leave at that point, even if some part of you desires that closeness.

Difficulty trusting others Another attachment issue may look like expecting loved ones to betray you or abandon you, even without a clear reason for having such an expectation. When you expect betrayal or abandonment, it makes it hard to trust others because you could be hurt at any moment. This leads to not trusting or committing to others.

Emotional extremes A person with attachment issues might also experience emotional extremes such as intense affection followed by withdrawal. This push and pull is often the result of having a deep desire to connect but also carrying fears of betrayal and abandonment.

Overreacting to rejection or separation In relationships, conflict occurs, and it can create emotional and physical distance. For a person with attachment issues, this state of affairs can result in experiencing huge feelings of anxiety or anger.

People-pleasing and conflict avoidance One of the outcomes of attachment issues is being afraid of conflict and disagreements. You may worry that they signal the beginning of the end, or even the end of the relationship itself. As such, a person with attachment issues may find themselves seeking the approval of others at their own expense just to avoid conflict or disagreement.

The patterns of attachment issues can appear in small and subtle ways, such as those described above. They can show up as constantly checking for messages from a loved one, struggling to relax and just be in friendships, or feeling a sense of dread or panic if someone seems distant. It can also look like overdependence on others’ reassurance. In work settings, it could also look like a reluctance to collaborate closely with colleagues.

Some Causes of Attachment Issues, and Their Impact on Life and Relationships

Attachment issues will often stem from early relational experiences, but later life experiences can also result in attachment issues. In large measure, attachment issues are connected to an insecure attachment style that’s formed when a person’s needs for safety, comfort, and connection are violated, neglected, or met inconsistently. Some of the early life experiences that can result in attachment issues include:

Neglect or Abandonment This is when physical or emotional needs go repeatedly unmet. If a child doesn’t feel seen, if the adults around them don’t respond to bids for attention or for play, the child may develop the understanding that their needs don’t matter.

Inconsistent caregiving Just as damaging is when a caregiver is sometimes present and nurturing, but sometimes neglectful. Such inconsistent caregiving makes the child see life as unpredictable, and their needs as something that can’t reliably be met by others.

Loss or Major Life Disruptions Experiencing separation from caregivers, whether through frequent moves, divorce, or death, can result in attachment issues.

Trauma or Abuse When a child experiences fear or harm in their close relationships, that may also lead to developing attachment issues.

As influential as these early experiences are, later life experiences can also either reinforce or cultivate difficulties with attachment. These experiences include betrayals, long-term stress in relationships, or toxic relationships.

When you have attachment issues, it has a huge impact on how you experience trust, love, and friendships. Different attachment issues may show up in various struggles, such as feeling secure in your relationships. You might not quite feel at ease, able to simply enjoy the relationship and be loved.

Attachment issues can also make it hard to maintain healthy boundaries with other people. Instead of being able to place healthy limits on yourself for your well-being, you might easily violate them to please others. With attachment issues, it can be harder to communicate your needs without feeling guilt or fear. Lastly, attachment issues can result in experiencing prolonged loneliness or anxiety.

The different patterns of behavior that are associated with attachment issues can put you in situations where you experience isolation in your relationships, relationship conflict, or emotional exhaustion from violating your own boundaries.

How to Overcome Attachment Issues

Your past doesn’t dictate your future. Attachment issues aren’t a life sentence that you have no choice but to live with them. Old fears can be overcome, and you can learn as well as re-learn connection and trust. There are effective strategies that can help you heal from and overcome attachment issues.

Some strategies you can consider include the following:

Nurturing healthy self-awareness Knowing yourself can be a powerful tool that can help you set and maintain healthy boundaries, as well as understand your own reactions to situations. Through practices such as journaling or mindfulness, you’ll learn how to identify your own emotional triggers and responses. This will help you as you try to manage your emotions and how you relate to others you’re in a relationship with.

Learning emotional regulation Being able to handle your own emotions can take practical steps. Getting adequate sleep and managing other emotional triggers are helpful. It also includes practicing techniques to help manage anxiety, anger, and fear. These include mindfulness, breathing techniques, and visualization.

Re-parenting yourself This can include treating yourself with compassion and providing yourself with the comfort and reassurance you may have lacked as a child. You are fearfully and wonderfully made in the image of the Creator, and you matter (Genesis 1:26-28; Psalm 8, 139; Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:16-19). Embracing the reality of God’s love for you can make a remarkable difference in your life.

Building safe connections Taking the time to cultivate relationships with supportive and trustworthy people can help you reset your expectations and ability to relate to others in a healthy way.

Counseling and therapy Healing from attachment issues is a gradual process, and it’s one that takes intentionality. With help from a counselor or therapist, you can identify your patterns of attachment issues. Your counselor or therapist might use approaches such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to not only identify those unhealthy patterns, but also to reframe any false and damaging beliefs you may have about relationships.

If you need support to work through your attachment issues, be sure to browse our online counselor directory or contact our reception team. A counselor can help you begin your journey to overcome attachment issues and the concerns they raise in your relationships.

item.title: Common Signs of Codependency in Relationships
item.description:
Relationships work best when two people connect, sharing their needs, working together to resolve problems, and showing a mutual appreciation of the differences that make them unique. Healthy relationships can abide differences, and they nurture the pursuit of one’s best self as the Lord envisions it. At their best, relationships help us to be more fully human.

Just as relationships have their benefits, they can also have a dark side. How people conduct themselves in relationships, and the way others relate to them, may not be healthy. Some patterns of speech, behavior, and attitudes can be devastating, not just for the relationship itself, but for the individuals in that relationship. Being attentive to and discerning of these patterns can help you identify and avoid unhealthy relationships.

Codependency is just one of many different unhealthy patterns of relationships. You may find that one or more of your relationships has a codependent dynamic, and for your sake and the sake of others around you, it’s important that you pinpoint that dynamic and find ways to turn things around.

Codependency and Its Root Causes

The word ‘codependent’ is likely vaguely familiar to you. To begin with, there’s nothing wrong with two people being mutually dependent on one another. In fact, there’s something beautiful about the way the Lord designed us to thrive through relationships. We are meant to live in community with others, sharing the best of ourselves with them (1 Corinthians 12; Matthew 22:34-40; John 13:34-35).

While mutual dependence is one thing, codependence points to something else entirely. When a person is codependent, they rely excessively on another person for things such as their identity, sense of self-worth, or emotional support. They might feel lost without the other person, unable to forge a path for their own life or follow their own priorities.

At first glance, it can be hard to draw a firm line between healthy reliance and excessive reliance. Relationships differ, and life often has fluid circumstances that make it complex and difficult to pin down. A partner or spouse who’s struggling with physical or mental impairment due to illness may be entirely dependent on their counterpart, and rightly so, even if it’s just for a season. A child is also dependent on a parent.

Codependency shows up in those relationships and situations where a person can be reasonably expected to establish their own sense of self, and they can meet significant emotional needs without reference to others. The excesses of codependency will typically show up in unhealthy patterns of enabling behavior, sacrificing oneself to meet others’ needs, being controlling over others, ultimately to the detriment of one’s well-being.

When it comes to the roots of codependency, it often traces back to formative early life experiences. If a person grows up in an environment where abuse, neglect, or inconsistent caregiving are the norm, they may develop low self-esteem and deep-seated fears of abandonment. They may not trust that what is here today will be here tomorrow, and that can induce anxieties and fear about the permanence of relationships.

These early life experiences can result in a codependent dynamic. The individual learns to draw lines between their value and how well they either please or care for others. Their sense of identity becomes attached to what they do for others, and their sense of purpose is tied to caring for others, even when that care is detrimental to their own well-being.

Signs of Codependency in Relationships

How can you identify patterns of codependency in your relationships? One of the challenges with identifying codependency is that it can easily be mistaken for being a nice person who is deeply loving and self-sacrificial. Codependency can be praised because it can look like being a saint. Knowing some of the signs of codependency can help you identify these tendencies and distinguish them from healthy self-giving.

Some of the common signs of codependency include the following:

Poor boundaries A boundary is a limit that indicates what you feel comfortable or uncomfortable doing, or it can be thought of as a psychological demarcation that distinguishes one individual from another. A person with poor boundaries can struggle to say ‘no’ to others’ requests or impositions. They may also feel responsible for others’ feelings or problems.

People-pleasing Codependency can also involve being eager to please people. You may be afraid to offend others and go out of your way to be inoffensive. It is rooted in an overwhelming need to gain the approval of other people, even when it comes at great personal expense.

Control issues A potentially surprising sign of codependency is the desire to manage others’ lives to feel secure. A codependent person often swoops in to rescue others, which can easily and quickly look like controlling them, their lives, and their choices.

Low self-esteem In a real way, a codependent person has a poorly developed sense of self. The result is that they might go through life measuring their self-worth through others’ opinions of them or the relational status they have.

Caretaking Another sign of codependency is feeling compelled to “fix” others’ lives and problems, especially when it is accompanied by neglecting one’s own needs.

Fear of abandonment Codependency might also be indicated when a person stays in unhealthy relationships out of fear of being alone.

Resentment Willingly serving others is one thing, but codependency often results in feelings of resentment toward them. Codependence leads to joyless, nearly servile attempts at meeting the needs of others. Doing things you really don’t want to be doing to earn the approval of others can wear on your soul and result in deep resentment toward them, and yourself as well, for going along with it.

The Spiritual Dangers of Codependency

In a codependent dynamic, there’s the party who always swoops in to rescue the other individual who’s perpetually in trouble, whether it be addiction, money problems, or bad relationships. The enabler is more than happy to allow the rescuer to rescue them, and that dynamic can continue uninterrupted for long seasons and cycles in their lives. There are dangers with a codependent dynamic, and some of these are spiritual in nature.

Codependency can pose subtle yet profound spiritual dangers, whether related to people-pleasing, poor boundaries, resentment, or the source of one’s identity. There is, for instance, a possibility of wandering into idolatry when you elevate people to a position of influence and authority that rightly belongs to the Lord alone.

When you root your identity in anything other than Christ, the likely result is disappointment, hurt, and disillusionment. The identity that you form from relationships, and the self-worth that’s rooted there instead of in Christ, isn’t a stable one, particularly because people can be fickle. The price that’s exacted may lead you into ungodliness to retain those relationships.

Prioritizing others’ needs to the point of neglecting your own doesn’t mirror who God is. Jesus was the quintessential servant-leader, but He was able to assert His own boundaries, contradict what was untrue, and take time for Himself to rest and pray (Mark 1:35; Mark 10:45; Matthew 22:23-33). Prioritizing others’ needs above your own or the Lord’s purposes for your life may result in spiritual neglect and distancing yourself from God.

Recovery from Codependency

The path toward recovery from codependency is possible. While codependency is rooted in a poor sense of self, it is possible to begin rooting your identity in Christ, helping you to reorient your life and nurture healthier relationships with good boundaries that promote well-being.

Some steps you can take:

Acknowledge the issue Ask the Lord for discernment to identify unhealthy patterns in your life and relationships.

Seek the Lord Rebuild your identity in Christ, including your sense of self-worth. Hear what the Lord has to say about you throughout Scripture (Galatians 2:20; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Romans 8; Psalm 139).

Establish healthy boundaries Healthy boundaries are necessary and promote mutual respect. Learn to say “No” without feeling guilty about it.

Prioritize self-care Prioritize your emotional, physical, and spiritual well-being as part of what it means to be a good steward of all that the Lord has given you.

Seek support Mentorship, support groups, and professional Christian counseling can help you on your journey. Such relationships can foster healing and accountability as you grow healthier, less codependent relationships.

To learn more about the signs of codependency and to schedule a consultation with a local counselor or therapist, contact our office today.

item.title: Life After Trauma: Adjusting to a New Normal
item.description:
When trauma hits, it feels like your whole world has come crashing down. And in some cases, that’s true. What you knew to be true isn’t. What you thought was concrete crumbled. Now you’re sitting there, in the aftermath of horror, trying to rebuild your life. It looks different. You look different. People may even treat you differently. Life after trauma is a weird, unnerving lens that now alters the way you see the world.

If you’re living in a tumultuous post-trauma period, you know how dark and lifeless, or how scary and animated the world has become. You long for normal. Not this new normal that feels dark and threatening, but the familiarity of your former life. You want life before the accident, the death, the divorce, the assault. While your former life wasn’t always perfect, you felt secure.

Why does the world look so different?

Trauma makes the world around you look different. Even familiar places and people might have a different feeling to them. Trauma changes you. Trauma makes you look at the world through a different lens entirely. Things that used to be benign are now a threat. The things that used to bring comfort don’t have that same transformative power.

Trauma also changes the people around you. Many people don’t know how to treat you after you’ve been through a life-changing event. Some people may rally to your side, offering hope, prayer, and a hug. Others will feel awkward and inadequate, so they avoid the topic of the trauma. They skirt deep conversations, only exchanging pleasantries. Or maybe they avoid you altogether, trying to shield themselves from their own triggers or awkwardness.

Sometimes trauma also changes your environment. Maybe you can’t spend time with the people you used to before you lost your job or your marriage. Maybe you were forced to move because your house was foreclosed upon. Maybe you can’t go to the places you used to since you lost your ability to drive. Trauma can rob you of the familiar in ways that you may have never anticipated.

Trauma also changes your perspective. The world may be familiar, but it certainly doesn’t seem as beautiful. Your mind is clouded by what has happened and what might happen again. You can’t fully immerse yourself in the world around you.

Rewriting a New Normal After Trauma

While your old life may suddenly be unavailable to you due to circumstances, your life can still be beautiful, familiar, and full of opportunities. You may be living in a new place, surrounded by unfamiliar people or circumstances, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t thrive.

Trauma provides you with a unique opportunity to rewrite your life. You have the chance to eliminate those habits, people, or things that cause you to drift from God. It allows you to establish newer, healthier lifestyle choices and to explore new hobbies and places. Maybe it’s time to rekindle an old romance or to learn to knit. Maybe it’s time to travel or to go back to church. Maybe it’s time to reach out to an old friend and mend a broken relationship.

Trauma gives you a big reset button on your life. This allows you to script it in a way that serves you now, and that will carry you confidently into the future. The good news is that you, with God’s help, have control over how it is written. God, your loving Heavenly Father, has the power to turn your ashes into blooming, fruit-bearing trees.

Draw closer to God

The key to rewriting your life and establishing a new, safe, and familiar life is to draw closer to God. While others might have empathy for you and may understand what you’ve been through to a certain measure, God knows it all. He feels what you feel and knows what you think. And best of all, He loves you even in your darkest, weakest moments.

When you draw closer to God through prayers, Bible study, worship, and community, you will organically try to serve Him. Old habits that drew you away from God will suddenly not hold the same appeal. As the Holy Spirit enters your life, you begin to feel peace, strength, and clarity. Fear begins to melt and calm blankets your life.

This new peace, this relationship with your Creator, will heal the brokenness of the past. It will soften the edges and calm the triggers. As Paul writes, “Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6-7, NIV)

In this new, peaceful place, you can, with God’s help, build a new life. You might carry some friendships, some hobbies, and preferences into your new life, but the foundation will be built on the firm foundation of Christ.

Advantages of Trauma Survival

Unfortunately, trauma and sad, scary things hit almost everyone at some point in life. If you’re going through a trauma now, you know about all the negative and prickly parts of the experience. But have you ever thought about the advantages you now have that you’ve lived through a tragedy?

After you’ve lived through a big life event, you begin to have clarity. You are no longer in denial or naïve to the more difficult parts of life. You no longer pretend that life is easy or predictable because you’ve seen the cracks. And while this might not sound like a good thing, these moments of clarity make you wiser, more grounded, more compassionate, and more reliant on God.

You gain depth after trauma. Small talk might feel empty now, but meaningful conversations are powerful. You can recognize pain in others more quickly, and your empathy for them runs deeper. You notice who is hurting behind their masks because you know, firsthand, how it looks to carry hidden pain. This awareness allows you to love people with more intention and to extend grace where others might rush to judgment.

You also gain strength. Even if you don’t feel strong, the simple fact that you survived your trauma proves that you are. You’ve lived through days you never thought you would make it through. That strength won’t shield you from all of life’s traumas, but it proves that you can keep going even when you are faced with obstacles. Trauma survivors often underestimate their own courage because it was born out of necessity, not by choice.

Trauma also clarifies your priorities. Things that once consumed your energy, like status, appearance, approval, or busyness, often become less important to you after a trauma. You begin to value things like peace, family and friends, and purpose over frivolous possessions or empty productivity.

With all the hardships and agony you endured, you also gained a voice and a story. One day, when you’re ready, your story might become a lifeline for someone else. Your testimony of survival and God’s role in your life might be just the thing that draws others to Him. There is incredible power in saying, “I’ve been there, and you’re not alone.” God often uses our deepest wounds to bring about meaningful change in others.

Therapy for Trauma

Perhaps one of the most effective ways of rewriting your new life in a meaningful and positive way is through therapy. A Christian therapist can be a listening ear when you want to retell your trauma. They can be a trusted voice of reason when you’re analyzing your life in the aftermath, and they can teach you coping skills so that you can successfully deal with future crises in a positive, healthy way.

A Bright New Future

You might not see it now, with your eyes still clouded by the trauma you’ve endured, but your future is bright. It might not look exactly as it did before you went through your trauma, but that doesn’t mean it can’t be beautiful, productive, and prosperous.

God wants you to live an abundant life, filled with His presence. In the aftermath of your trauma, you have the unique opportunity to rescript your life in a way that pleases God and serves you and others. Start this process today by talking to a Christian counselor. Connect with the reception team to learn more.

item.title: The Effects of Trauma on Relationships and Mental Health
item.description:
Life hurts. The reality of living east of Eden is that life hurts, and it can hurt in many ways, with different results. Trauma is the emotional response a person has to an experience that overwhelms their ability to cope. The effects of trauma can linger for days, months, or even years, disrupting the individual’s ability to function and their well-being.

When you understand trauma as well as how it can affect you, your mental health, and your relationships, it’s a great first step to putting measures in place to begin healing. There are different types of trauma and traumatic events, and they affect individuals in varied and deeply personal ways.

Types of Trauma and Traumatic Events

Trauma and traumatic events come in different guises. Trauma can be the result of complex life experiences, but it can also be the result of a single event or experiences of ongoing abuse. When a person faces traumatic events and becomes traumatized by them, they can respond in a variety of ways.

They may respond with resilience in the face of such challenges, walking gradually toward recovery. They may also be distressed and require professional support for their well-being.

There are several ways to categorize trauma. One common way to do this is by addressing the nature and the duration of exposure to the traumatic event. The main types of trauma that arise from different kinds of life-threatening or distressing experiences are acute, chronic, and complex trauma.

Acute trauma stems from a sudden, single event that’s highly distressing. This sort of event disrupts a person’s sense of safety, upending how secure they feel in everyday life. Acute trauma can be caused by events like witnessing a violent crime, the unexpected death of a loved one, being subjected to sexual or physical assault, getting caught up in a natural disaster like wildfire, or undergoing a life-threatening illness or serious injury.

The second kind of trauma, chronic trauma, is the sort that arises when one is repeatedly exposed to the trauma over a long period of time. That period could be months or years, and it includes experiences like persistent harassment or bullying, facing chronic illness or an ongoing medical issue, long-term emotional, sexual, or physical abuse, or living in a violent neighborhood or in a warzone.

Complex trauma is a third kind of trauma, and it is often quite severe. It can be the result of varied, multiple, and prolonged traumatic events. These events will often carry a sense of being trapped and feeling unable to escape the situation. Situations such as childhood abuse, prolonged exposure to domestic abuse, being trafficked, or experiencing torture or refugee trauma are examples of complex trauma.

Other forms of trauma would include what’s known as intergenerational trauma, which references trauma responses being transmitted across generations. People who’ve been exposed to trauma such as war, colonization, or systemic racism may pass on their trauma responses to their descendants.

Another form of trauma is secondary or vicarious trauma. This form of trauma typically affects individuals in the helping professions who are repeatedly exposed to other people’s suffering and trauma. This would include social workers, medical personnel, first responders, and others who witness and are exposed to others’ traumatic experiences.

Trauma may also be named depending on when it occurs. There is a category of trauma which is called adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). These potentially traumatic experiences that a child undergoes have a lasting impact well into adulthood. They include experiences like neglect, abuse, and parental abandonment.

How Trauma Affects Your Mental Health and Relationships

Depending on the context, duration, and intensity of the traumatic experience a person undergoes, the impact will vary. The impact of traumatic events will also depend on other factors, such as one’s personality and the support system they have around themselves. Trauma affects you mentally, emotionally, and physically. Not only that, but trauma also affects daily life as well as your relationships with other people.

One of the main ways that trauma affects a person is by disrupting their sense of safety, self-worth, and trust. Mentally and emotionally, trauma creates challenges such as emotional dysregulation. This is when a person is unable to handle their own emotions, including soothing themselves. Trauma can result in anger, shame, sadness, and even intense fear, but it can also result in emotional numbness and feeling disconnected.

Trauma can also have these effects:

Withdrawal and avoidance To avoid reminders of the trauma, a traumatized person may steer clear of people, places, situations, or even sounds and smells that trigger trauma and have associations with the trauma. Many survivors step back from hobbies and communal activities. Avoidance and withdrawal often result in difficulties maintaining relationships and one’s social support system.

Changes in self-perception When a person is traumatized, it can change how they perceive themselves as well as the world they inhabit. Imagine what it’s like to be caught up in a natural disaster. What may have felt familiar and reliable starts to feel unsafe or unstable. If it’s relational trauma, feelings such as guilt, self-blame, and mistrust of others may set in.

Intrusive memories and thoughts One sign of trauma and how it’s affecting a person is when they experience flashbacks, distressing memories of the event, or nightmares. These memories and thoughts make them relive the traumatic event over and over. This can be quite disturbing and deeply unsettling for one’s focus and emotional stability.

Hyperarousal Trauma can lead to one’s body responding as though it is under constant threat. This makes it hard to rest, and you’re easily startled. Hyperarousal makes a person feel constantly on edge and unable to settle.

Health problems Putting your body under constant stress will affect your body and lead to health problems. When trauma isn’t resolved, it increases the risk of health conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, and heart disease. Trauma can show up as unexplained ailments such as fatigue, chronic pain, headaches, and gastrointestinal concerns.

Relational difficulties The trust issues trauma nurtures can result in a fear of intimacy, as well as finding it hard to form and maintain relationships with other people. Someone who has experienced trauma will often find it hard to express their emotional needs. They may withdraw during conflict or misinterpret their partner’s actions as threatening.

Relationships may become strained because of trauma. One’s partner may feel rejected, overwhelmed, and confused. That might lead to even greater distance in the relationship. Even one’s parenting can be affected. A traumatized parent may become detached from their child or overprotective. They may also struggle to manage their child’s emotional needs.

Work strain Just as trauma can affect personal relationships, it can also affect how a person functions in professional settings, whether at work or school. Decision-making and sustaining focus become harder due to trauma; even maintaining regular routines or socializing can become overwhelming. Trauma can impact how you interact with other people, and that includes at work.

A trauma survivor can become anxious in team environments; they may be overly cautious or even highly sensitive to criticism from authority figures. Issues such as emotional outbursts, missed deadlines, absenteeism, and difficulty collaborating with others can all make for a challenging professional life. Isolation may be the result, as well as limited opportunities for advancement.

Unhealthy coping mechanisms The overwhelming emotions unleashed by a traumatic experience can be hard to process and handle in a healthy way. For some survivors, alcohol, drugs, risky behaviors like unsafe driving or casual liaisons, or self-harm become ways to cope. These, however, aren’t healthy ways to cope. They complicate healing from trauma, and they can cause significant damage.

Finding Help to Overcome Trauma

It’s possible to recover from trauma with time. However, for some, their symptoms persist or even worsen, and that’s a good indicator that you need to seek professional help. Trauma counselors or therapists can walk with you using evidence-based treatments and therapies. In some instances, prescribed medication may be necessary to tamp down the impact of the symptoms of trauma.

With the help of a trauma counselor or therapist, you can rebuild your sense of safety, stability, and the healthy relationships that help you stay connected and that nurture well-being. Talk to someone immediately if you’re distressed and have thoughts of self-harm. Help is available through a crisis line or by calling emergency services.

Consider working with a counselor to find hope and healing from your trauma. Connect with this office to set up an initial consultation.

item.title: Tips for Body Image Disorder from a Christian Counseling Perspective
item.description:
Body image disorder, or body dysmorphic disorder, affects roughly 2% of adults in the U.S. Body image is your perceptions, attitudes, behaviors, and thoughts about your body. Your beliefs about your appearance can stem from childhood, trauma, or recent events.

Body image disorder is a negative perception of your body. You see your body differently from how it is. You become preoccupied with thoughts regarding your appearance, body shape, size, or weight. You may spend hours in front of the mirror or spend excessive amounts of money trying to fix any perceived flaws. You may excessively diet and exercise.

Body image disorder can lead to anxiety, depression, negative thoughts, isolation, and compulsive behaviors. Counseling is still one of the primary treatments for the condition.

Tips for Body Image Disorder

Combining lifestyle changes with counseling can help you manage the symptoms of body image disorder. A few take consistent daily practice, while others are things you can schedule into your calendar when you have time. Pick some of the lifestyle changes and tips below to get started.

  • Step Back from Social Media – Social media can feed our negative thoughts and emotions about our bodies. We cannot help but compare our appearances to highly edited and filtered versions of others. We forget that not everyone on social media is in a healthy mental space. Take a small sabbatical from social media or limit your interaction to checking messages and notifications only once a day for a while.
  • Appreciate All of You – Positive affirmations are a great way to shift your mindset and accept your body and appearance. Write out a few affirmations to say in the morning while looking in the mirror. You can also carry them with you in the note app on your phone to say throughout the day.
  • Join a Support Group – You need support while seeking treatment for body image disorder. Join a local or online support group of others familiar with the condition. This group should be led by a counselor or someone who has overcome poor body image. The participants can lean on each other and offer support.
  • Help Others – Get outside yourself and your thoughts by volunteering to help others. Check with your church or local community center for opportunities. If you struggle with social interactions due to body image disorder, challenge yourself to serve others for a small period of time, such as 30 minutes to an hour.
  • Reframe Negative Thoughts – Negative thoughts can lead to compulsive behaviors and negative emotions. You can take control of your behaviors by reframing your thoughts to ones that are more conducive to health and body positivity.
  • Do Something Fun with a Friend – Focusing too much on appearance is detrimental to mental health. Try activities that focus your mind on someone or something else. Do something fun with a friend, such as meet at a coffee shop, try a painting class, check out a classic car show, or hike.

Choose one or two tips to try first. Also, consider getting help from a professional with experience in this area.

Christian Counseling is Available for Body Image Disorder

To manage body image disorder, you need to identify the cause and learn how to process those emotions while shifting to a healthier mental space with positive coping mechanisms. Managing body image disorder through Christian counseling takes time as you tackle obstacles, learn to love and accept your body, and make healthy choices through a faith-based lens.

Connect with us today to schedule a session with a Christian counselor specializing in body image disorder.

item.title: Finding Support When You’re Battling Severe Depression Symptoms
item.description:
Whether you have battled severe depression symptoms on and off for years or were just diagnosed, there is light at the end of the tunnel. You can alleviate depression symptoms through lifestyle changes and professional help from a mental health care provider.

Severe Depression Symptoms Require Professional Help

Severe depression symptoms can feel as if they will never go away. Perhaps you have been fighting depressive episodes for years. This type of depression requires professional help. Negative thoughts influence emotions and behavior and can contribute to an increase in severe depression symptoms.

Genetics, family history, brain chemical imbalances, major life events, and environmental factors can also combine to raise your risk. Your physician will take an assessment and may prescribe medication to help you through as you seek therapy.

Counseling

Counseling provides you with an outlet in a safe place to find words for your feelings. What you say is confidential, and your counselor can help provide insight. Specific psychological methods have been proven effective for alleviating depression and anxiety. You will work with your counselor to create a mental health care plan and set goals for treatment.

The number of sessions needed is customized. You may see a change in your severe depression symptoms with weekly sessions over the course of a few months. Depending on your counselor, you may attend a combination of in-person and virtual sessions as well as phone calls or text messages for check-ins throughout the week or if needed.

Talk Therapy

Talk therapy helps you uncover what is behind your depression. Sometimes getting to the bottom of a situation and finding solutions can relieve depression and anxiety.

For example, your schedule, finances, and relationship with your spouse may fuel your depression. Your counselor can work with you to set boundaries, delegate and delete tasks, set financial goals, and rebuild your relationship with your spouse, so that you feel more in control of your life, taking an intentional step forward instead of a reactive step.

Group Therapy

Millions of people in the United States suffer from depression. You are not alone. Group therapy brings others together in a controlled environment. Participants agree that anything said is confidential. You can feel free to share your struggles and your wins. Your story or advice may help someone else.

Group therapy is led by a mental health practitioner and may include talk therapy and group counseling activities. Sessions are typically in-person, but some counselors host virtual sessions for participants who can’t make face-to-face appointments or who prefer to meet from home.

Medication

Although your counselor will not prescribe medication, your physician may add an antidepressant regimen for severe depression symptoms. Consult with your pharmacist about any new medications and any interactions with current medications.

Medication combined with healthy lifestyle changes, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), and counseling can help you beat depression symptoms by learning how to minimize the effects.

Changing Your Habits to Alleviate Severe Depression Symptoms

Often, the lifestyle choices we make have a direct effect on our mental health. Substances like alcohol and drugs, caffeine, and ultra-processed foods could exacerbate symptoms. Turning healthier changes into habits takes time.

To solidify a new habit, add it to an existing one. This “habit stacking” has been found to make it easier to follow through. For example, if you want to start journaling before bed, attach the habit to something you do every night, such as brushing your teeth or changing into your pajamas. Brush your teeth and then immediately sit down to journal for five or ten minutes.

Adopt a sleep schedule and routine

Not enough good-quality sleep can worsen depression. Depression can either make you sleep too much or develop insomnia. Counteract these sleep issues with a sleep schedule and routine. Choose three to four tasks that you will do every night before bed to signal to your mind that it is time to wind down. For example, put away your phone, take a shower, brew a cup of herbal tea, and read a book.

Aim for seven to nine hours of sleep nightly, if possible. If you are a night owl, trying to scale back to an earlier bedtime too fast probably won’t work. Instead, cut back by fifteen minutes for one week at a time. If you normally go to bed at 11 pm, aim for 10:45 pm over the next week, then 10:30 pm the week after. Eventually, your mind and body will catch up and know it’s time for sleep.

Eat nutritious foods

Too many ultra-processed foods can disrupt the neurotransmitters responsible for regulating mood. These types of foods promote chronic inflammation, which can lead to cognitive issues and depression.

Choose whole foods at least 80% to 90% of the time, allowing yourself treats for the remaining 10% to 20% of your food consumption. Prioritize protein, healthy fats, whole grains, and fresh fruits and vegetables. Establish a menu for the week before grocery shopping to ensure you have plenty of healthy options on hand.

Get consistent with exercise

Boost your mood and outlook with regular exercise. Heart-pumping workouts can lift your mood, improve your confidence, boost cognitive function, and improve heart and lung function. Your physical and mental health benefit from exercise. Consult with your physician before starting any new exercise regimen.

For overall health, aim for 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise weekly. You will notice your mood lifting, pain decreasing, confidence growing, and physical health improving. You may also lose excess weight and find that your appetite regulates.

Avoid alcohol and drugs

Although alcohol and drugs can temporarily make you forget your worries, numb emotional pain, or boost your mood, these sensations never last. Only a deep dive into why you are depressed and the acquisition of new skills will reduce those thoughts and emotions.

Some people can stop substance abuse immediately. Others require help from a professional. Don’t hesitate to ask for help if alcohol or drugs have become a coping mechanism.

Journal your thoughts and feelings

Journaling is an excellent exercise for delving deep and identifying negative thoughts that may be fueling your depression. On the page, you can analyze and strategize how to handle these thoughts and behaviors. You can also share your journal entries with your counselor.

Journaling also enables you to identify behavioral patterns. Do you feel more depressed after dealing with a specific person or attending an event? Take note of how you feel throughout the day and write down what you were doing or thinking when your mood dropped.

Join a support group

A support group provides a place to offer and receive encouragement and advice. A support group is typically led by either a mental health practitioner or an individual who has managed depression for a long time. These people are familiar with the challenges and triggers.

Some support groups engage in activities, such as the trust jar. Each participant writes a struggle on a slip of paper and drops it into the jar anonymously. Someone retrieves a slip randomly from the jar, and the group gives their input on how to manage the problem. No one feels put on the spot, and everyone can participate.

Find one thing you love and do it

Depression can rob you of the pleasure you once held for certain activities. Take that joy back by finding one thing you love and doing it, even if you don’t feel up to it. Sometimes, half the battle is getting started.

Don’t feel like meeting friends at the movies? Invite someone over to your house for a movie instead. Used to love reading, and now nothing holds your interest? Find a short novella or short story and read it. Give yourself at least two minutes to do something you always enjoyed before stopping for the day.

Next Steps

Seek help immediately if your severe depression symptoms feel uncontrollable or if you are having thoughts of self-harm or suicide. This is not a fight you have to go through alone. Call us today to speak to a representative about depression, and we will connect you to a Christian counselor near you. Let us walk with you through this season.

item.title: Rediscovering Your Sense of Self After Divorce
item.description:
Anytime relationships are severed, no matter the reason, you’re bound to feel a loss. This is true, even when the loss comes voluntarily or after a toxic relationship ends. After a divorce, it’s normal to feel the absence of your partner, but the losses don’t end there. Sometimes you can also feel the loss of self.

For the duration of your marriage, and probably a few years before that, you’ve been defined as a couple. Invitations came in both your names, as did the monthly bills. You signed Christmas cards as a duo, and the word we ruled your vocabulary. Suddenly, you’re solo, and walking into a party by yourself feels awkward. You think back to the time before you were a we and wonder how you ever felt comfortable in your own skin, standing alone.

Here you are, again, being an I or a me, but it feels different. The last time you were single was different. Today, you feel self-conscious about sitting in a coffeehouse alone, which was a regular occurrence before your relationship.

You become acutely aware of the eyes following you as you walk around the grocery store alone. In your former single life, those eyes felt more flirtatious than judgmental. You glance at the couple holding hands and talking about dinner. You even feel a twinge of envy prick at your heart and wonder if you will ever be part of a couple again.

Where did I go?

Losing your identity can happen slowly. It can be so slow that you might not realize that it happened at all until you’re confronted with it. Divorce has a way of doing that. It shines a light on your aloneness. And when you step back to examine what your life is like in this new season, what you are like in this new season, it can lead to some rather surprising discoveries.

Before marriage, most people have a defined set of beliefs, a few hobbies they enjoy, friends they like to mingle with, and goals that keep them going. But through marriage, many times these two individual lives meld into one. And that’s a good thing.

God designed marriage where “…the two will become one flesh.” (Mark 10:8, NIV) But when something goes awry and these two melded individuals part ways, it can be challenging.

Suddenly, you realize that your pre-marriage self doesn’t really exist anymore. Your beliefs may have changed and evolved. This can be from age and maturity, but also the influence of a spouse. And those hobbies that you used to engage in, well, they might still be there, but maybe you haven’t done them in a while.

Friends may have drifted away because you didn’t have time for them, or simply because their lives pulled them in a different direction. And your individual goals somehow got absorbed into mutual goals, morphing into something either undesirable or unattainable as a single.

Where did I go? You might ask yourself. The I that you identified with is no longer there, or so it seems. You may even look different due to aging, stress, and influence from your partner. When you no longer look or feel like yourself, a disturbing realization can surprise you. You may feel that you no longer exist in your traditional and familiar form, and this can knock you right off your feet.

Why It Matters

Everyone changes, right? So, why would it matter that you’ve changed so much since the last time you were single? Everyone grows, evolves, and ages, even those who are single. The difference is that when you evolve as a single person, you are evolving on your own terms.

You are following a path that you have chosen, and that will serve you well as a single person. God has directed you down a path toward your individual goals. But when you think you will spend the rest of your life with someone, your evolution happens in tandem. Once you’re married, your financial goals merge, as do your life plans. When you’re suddenly single again, those mutual goals may not be relevant or even possible anymore.

This matters because divorce not only strips you of your relationship with your spouse but also forces you to redefine yourself as a person. You’re standing in the middle of your so-called life that feels oddly familiar and partly foreign, wondering what to do next.

It’s okay to mourn the loss of your relationship and all the things that were taken away with it. It is to be expected. Grieve the person you were, the person you were becoming, and the life that you had hoped would someday materialize.

A Challenge or an Opportunity

Don’t live in the mourning too long. You may catch yourself hesitating before making decisions because, for so long, you had to consider another person. Now, every small choice, even down to what to eat for dinner, is yours alone to make. Is it sad? Maybe a little, but it’s also a conduit to opportunities.

While it’s understandable to want to mourn your losses, you can’t dwell there forever. Moving on with your life is the goal. Some people would give a lot of hard-earned cash to have the opportunity to redefine themselves midlife. When your new label is divorcee, you might be met with a few challenges, of course, but you are also given a beautiful opportunity to rework your image, revamp your schedule, and renew your relationships.

You can prioritize the things you want to focus on, like a relationship with God, because you are no longer tied to another person who may have held you back. Divorce may be an end, but it also presents you with the opportunity for a beautiful beginning.

Moving on can be scary, not just after divorce but after any life change. But moving on will give you new friendships, new hobbies, and new goals to strive for. God doesn’t condone all divorce; in fact, He champions lifelong commitments.

But God is always faithful to meet you in your brokenness. He meets you when the ground beneath your feet feels shaky and unfamiliar. He loves you when grief and fear weigh heavily on your chest, and He can define you when you can’t remember who you are without someone else by your side.

God might not take away all your pain in an instant, but He is faithful to show you that even in this place, you are whole in Him.

Therapy can help

Your therapist can partner with you in this process of becoming whole again. God uses people in practical ways to help you process your new life and recover from your old one. A therapist can help you separate who you are from who you were when you were with someone else.

Through therapy sessions, you can see parts of yourself that may have been neglected. You might rediscover passions that were set aside and help you find the inner strength that has been waiting quietly for you to discover.

Single and Loving It

Reclaiming your true self, or better yet, redefining a refined version of you, doesn’t require going backward or resurrecting the person you were before marriage. You can step into a new version of you that has been shaped by experience, forged by pain, revived by hope, and growing in faith.

Of course, there will still be days when grief or doubt or self-consciousness will crash in unwelcomed, but through the grace of God and a little help from your therapist, you can walk intentionally into a new life. You can discover a life built with purpose and filled with the people, places, and things that serve you well in this season.

Soon you will be able to look back at your marriage, not with guilt or anger, but in appreciation for what you had and for what it helped you become. “Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance. Let perseverance finish its work so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.” (James 1:2-4, NIV)

While divorce should never be the end goal of marriage, God has a wonderful way of turning our trials into blessings. He uses these moments, these sad, lonely, desperate moments, to remind you of His love and faithfulness to you. Let a therapist help you on that journey. Connect with us today.

item.title: What To Do When You Feel Depressed
item.description:
Depression can feel like a real person, a tangible thing that you can almost touch. Depression and sadness are emotions. Sometimes, when you feel depressed, these feelings are due to circumstances, negative thoughts and beliefs, trauma, grief and loss, or a chemical imbalance.

This article gives suggestions on what to do when you feel depressed. If you are depressed and are having suicidal thoughts or are self-harming, seek help immediately.

When You Feel Depressed

Sometimes, a lifestyle tweak or new habit can get you back on track. The following are several suggestions for what to do when you feel depressed.

Get outdoors

A breath of fresh air can lift your mood. Try to spend a few minutes outside daily. Research shows that greener spaces can lower cortisol and decrease stress. Make walks to the park or hikes at a nearby trail part of your routine.

Call a friend

When something bothers you, reach out to a trusted friend to discuss your emotions. Often, we bury our feelings. Eventually, these hidden feelings emerge in other ways, perhaps through depression, anxiety, or physical conditions. Engage with friends when you feel down, either through phone calls or in person.

Exercise

Exercise can lift mood, reduce blood pressure, lower heart rate, and strengthen the heart, lungs, muscles, and bones. Aim for 30 minutes a few days a week. Even a brisk 10-minute walk will help boost your mood if you are new to it.

Do something for someone else

Depression can make us turn our focus inward. To battle this, do something for someone else. Volunteer in the community, serve in the church, write a get-well card to a friend, or visit people in the hospital or local nursing homes. You can also find volunteer opportunities in your local community online.

Eat a healthy and balanced meal

Preservatives and added chemicals have been linked to processed food, according to studies. Aim to eat as many balanced and healthy meals as you can. These meals should include lean protein, complex carbohydrates, fruits, vegetables, and healthy fats.

Get creative

Daily schedules can leave little time for creative pursuits, yet our minds yearn for creativity. Get creative in your endeavors. Ask yourself what hobbies and interests you love and get back to doing those things that bring your heart joy. Schedule them into your calendar just like you do for an important appointment. Your mental health will thank you.

Spend time with God

When the spirit, mind, and body are out of sync, it can leave you feeling down. The soul was created to commune with God. Spend time in His Word, study daily devotionals, pray, and worship Him. You will notice that the more time you give back to God, the more time and joy He gives to you.

Decide what activities you want to do when you feel depressed and create a routine with consistency. The more you practice these tips, the more you will reduce depression symptoms.

Seek Help From Christian Counseling in Los Angeles

After reading through the suggestions for what to do when you feel depressed, you now have a list of practical ways to alleviate those feelings of depression and sadness. However, if you need extra support, seek help from a Christian counselor. Our team can connect you to a counselor right away and schedule a session either in person or virtually.

Give us a call today to get started.

item.title: Adult Attachment Styles: How to Know Your Attachment Style
item.description:
Who are you in your relationships? Each individual has a different way they inhabit and express themselves in their relationships. A variety of factors influence this style, including formative past experiences. Adult attachment styles are an important way to discuss how people form and maintain their relationships, and help understand how to nurture healthier relationships.

When you understand yourself better, you can discern the patterns, challenges, and areas that require change and growth in your relationships. Your attachment style plays a significant role in your relationships, and understanding the style that best captures your relationship patterns can be a game-changer for you.

Attachment Styles in Brief

What is an attachment style? One way to break down this important concept is to say that it is the set of relational and emotional patterns that you develop and use in your interactions and relationships with others. The attachment pattern that best maps out your behaviors functions like an unconscious template that governs how you relate to others as an adult.

Your particular attachment style is primarily developed in your childhood. It developed based on how safe and connected you felt with your primary caregivers. Whatever pattern you enter into adulthood with isn’t permanent. This is important to note because the alternative would lead to despair. Thankfully, you can change things, even those set in place during your childhood.

Your attachment style influences how you deal with conflict, how you love others, how you receive love, and how you handle intimacy and independence from others. The different attachment styles will be explored further shortly.

The Different Attachment Styles

There are four types of attachment styles, all of which play a role in how we communicate, connect with others, and respond to intimacy. These attachment styles, including brief descriptions of them as well as how they might impact relationships, are as follows:

Secure attachment This form of attachment most often develops in childhood when a child’s caregivers are loving, consistent, physically present, and emotionally available. When the child expresses their needs, whether it’s for food, comfort, attention, or play, the needs are consistently met. As a result, the child carries the expectation that it’s okay to express needs, and those needs will be met.

An adult with secure attachment style will typically be comfortable with both independence and intimacy. They can trust others with themselves, and because they can share their emotions and thoughts as well as emotionally regulate themselves, they can communicate and manage conflict well. They can receive and give love in a balanced and healthy way.

The impact this sort of attachment style has on relationships is that those relationships will likely be stable, nurturing, and balanced. These are the sorts of relationships where both freedom and closeness are appreciated.

Avoidant (dismissive) attachment One of the insecure forms of attachment is avoidant attachment. This form of attachment most often develops in situations where a child’s caregivers are critical, emotionally distant, or unavailable. The child learns to depend on themselves and not on others, as others may not reliably meet their needs.

When an adult has an avoidant attachment style, they will often be quite self-reliant, and they may feel uncomfortable being emotionally intimate with others. Instead, they’ll tend to suppress their emotions. In times of stress, their default may be to distance themselves from others.

In a relationship, an avoidant adult will often engage in emotionally shallow relationships, avoiding deeper connections with and reliance on others. The avoidant partner may disconnect easily from their partner, and their partner, in turn, can feel shut out.

Anxious (preoccupied) attachment A second form of insecure attachment is anxious attachment. When a parent or caregiver is inconsistent with their care, that can result in this form of attachment. When the caregiver is sometimes distant but sometimes attentive and present, this can leave the child feeling uncertain about their position and security.

For the adult with anxious attachment, they may crave to be close to others. This, incidentally, distinguishes them from the avoidant attachment style. While craving closeness and reassurance, the anxious partner also fears being abandoned. They are highly sensitive to changes in their partner’s mood or behavior and can easily interpret actions as rejection or a prelude to abandonment.

The impact this attachment style could have on relationships includes excessive clinginess to one’s partner. The anxious partner may also tend to overthink. They navigate emotional highs and lows as they draw near, then withdraw as they experience what feels like rejection.

They may require excessive reassurances, even testing their partner’s affections and commitment, which can derail things.

Disorganized (fearful-avoidant) attachment The last major type of attachment style is the disorganized attachment style. The individuals who have this style of attachment often developed in an environment where there was neglect, abuse, or trauma. In those settings, their caregiver may have functioned as a source of both fear and of comfort.

When an adult has a disorganized form of attachment, they will often experience and express their inner conflict. They may desire closeness or intimacy, but they also fear being vulnerable. This can result in a pendulum swing from withdrawing, on the one hand, to seeking intimacy, on the other, without rhyme or reason.

In a relationship, the disorganized attachment style may lead to unstable or unpredictable bonds. There will often be confusion and mistrust in the relationship, leading to a lot of unintended hurt.

These main attachment styles are broad descriptions of how people relate to others in relationships and the patterns they follow. A given individual may have elements of the different styles and relate differently to others depending on the person they are in a relationship with. These attachment styles will often be defaults that a person reverts to, particularly in times of stress or conflict.

How to Move Toward Healthier Relationships

Take the time to acknowledge and discern your attachment style. Set aside your ideas and intentions in your relationships, and honestly examine how you act in relationships. When your partner doesn’t text you back immediately, what goes through your mind? Are you okay with the silence, or do you start to fill the gaps with ideas about what the silence means? Is your default to resist sharing your thoughts and feelings?

The way to move toward healthier relationships involves growing in self-awareness of your relationship patterns. Your childhood experiences may be influential, but they aren’t definitive or a final word on where your story will end. Growth is possible, and it requires emotional and spiritual work.

Take some time to consider your childhood and how you tend to respond to others in relationships today. Ask the Holy Spirit to unearth the patterns in your life, and the patterns your heart tends to default to. Other steps include the following:

Seek supportive, healthy relationships Nurturing healthy connections with friends, mentors, family, and partners who display emotional maturity and health is essential. These are people who aren’t emotionally reactive, who can freely share their feelings and thoughts with others (not as a way to manipulate or control them), and who handle conflict well. When you learn to be vulnerable in the right environment, that can result in growth.

Share yourself openly and honestly You can, in those safe and supportive relationships, practice expressing your needs and feelings without fear or defensiveness. When you share yourself openly, and you receive empathy and understanding, it builds secure bonds and promotes better dialogue in the relationship.

Seek healing from the Lord Your past can define you if you let it. Where does your help, ultimate security, and identity come from? That security, sense of self, ought to be rooted in the Lord. He will never abandon or forsake you (Psalm 27:10), and He is the only unchanging reality that you can build your entire life upon. Allow Him to redefine your sense of worth, as well as your sense of security.

Consider professional counseling Professional Christian counseling can be profoundly helpful in understanding secure attachment patterns and moving toward healthier relationships. Your counselor can help you explore Scripture as well as cognitive and therapeutic strategies that help you overcome unhealthy patterns. With that kind of help, you can cultivate more secure attachment patterns in your relationships.

When you embark upon your journey, be patient with yourself. The patterns of relating that you default to were formed over time; they are familiar and comfortable, even when they aren’t helpful. Not only should you be patient with yourself, but you should also take opportunities to celebrate even small steps toward intimacy, trust, healthy independence, and learning mutual respect in your relationships.

You can have healthy relationships, and a healthy, secure attachment style that undergirds such relationships. It’s possible to experience wholeness, safety, trust, and joy in your relationships, as the Lord intended. If you need help with relationships, reach out and connect with a Christian counselor near you or on this site.
